source_quote: Bleeding or spotting between menstrual periods. This can be caused by something other than endometriosis. If it happens often, you should see your doctor.
note: Weak because the source itself qualifies it in the same breath — "This can be caused by something other than endometriosis." Treating it as strong support would read more into the sentence than it says.

source_quote: Short menstrual cycles (27 days or fewer)
note: IMPERFECT MAPPING. The source's threshold is 27 days; our buckets break at 21 and 35. under_21_days sits inside "27 days or fewer" so the row is true, but it misses cycles of 21-27 days, which the source would also count. Fixing this properly means changing the feature's buckets, which would invalidate other rows — flagged rather than silently fudged.

source_quote: Infertility, or not being able to get pregnant.
note: Listed among the symptoms, but weak: infertility is non-specific and appears under PCOS too, so it separates the differential very little. Retires a previously dead-weight feature.

source_quote: Painful bowel movements or pain when urinating during menstrual periods. In rare cases, you may also find blood in your stool or urine.
note: Cyclical bowel and bladder pain is distinctive: the timing tie to menstruation is what makes it point at endometriosis rather than at a bowel or urinary condition.

source_quote: Pain during or after sex. This is usually described as a "deep" pain and is different from pain felt at the entrance to the vagina when penetration begins.
note:
Strong because the source goes out of its way to distinguish deep from entrance pain, which is characteristic framing rather than a bare list entry. The NHS endometriosis page corroborates: "pain during or after sex".
CORRECTED 2026-08-04. This note previously claimed the feature was "one of the most discriminating in the differential — neither PCOS nor fibroids is characterised by it". That was WRONG: the NHS fibroids page lists "pain or discomfort during sex" among fibroid symptoms. The row itself stands, but the feature separates endometriosis from fibroids far less than claimed, and uterine_fibroids now carries its own row for it.

source_quote: Pain. This is the most common symptom. Women with endometriosis may have many different kinds of pain.
note: THE ELIMINATION ROW for endometriosis. The source frames pain as THE most common symptom, not merely one entry in a list — characteristic framing, which is what the protocol requires before an argues_against row may be written. Without it, endometriosis never drops out of the differential. Note this is weaker grounds than the PCOS elimination row: "most common" is a statement about frequency, not a diagnostic criterion. If you think that is too thin, drop this row and accept that endometriosis will need a positive finding elsewhere to be eliminated.

source_quote: Very painful menstrual cramps. The pain may get worse over time.
note: Weak rather than strong because "very painful" is not a severity scale and our severe level means "stops you doing normal activities". The row covers part of what the source says; the progression over time has no feature.

source_quote: Chronic (long-term) pain in the lower back and pelvis
note: Endometriosis pain is not confined to periods, which is part of what separates it from ordinary period pain. Weak because "chronic" describes duration rather than the constant-through-the-cycle pattern our value names.

source_quote: Pelvic pain, which often happens during your period
note: Named as THE main symptom: the source introduces it with "The main symptoms of endometriosis are:". Corroborated by the Office on Women's Health, which says "Pain. This is the most common symptom."

source_quote: Menstrual periods that last more than seven days
note: Exact mapping onto our over_7_days bucket, which is rare and worth noting. Weak because the source lists it under "You might be more likely to get endometriosis if you have" — a risk factor, not a presenting sign.

source_quote: Irregular or heavy, painful periods are not normal.
note: Applied only at the top of the scale, not to "heavy", because MedlinePlus states a normal period "can be light or heavy". Soaking through protection every hour is the level NHS uses to define heavy periods and the level its escalation rules key on, so that is where the line is drawn.

source_quote: A woman's periods are irregular if the gap between them is less than 21 days or more than 35 days.
note: Stated as a definition of abnormality, so the complement is a definition of normality. The boundaries land exactly on our bucket edges, which means no approximation is involved in this row — rare, and worth noting.

source_quote: A woman's periods are irregular if the gap between them is less than 21 days or more than 35 days.
A woman's periods are irregular if the gap between them is less than 21 days or more than 35 days.
Irregular or heavy, painful periods are not normal.
note:
SOURCE CONFLICT, flagged rather than resolved silently. The Office on Women's Health says plainly that irregular periods "are not normal". The NHS irregular periods page opens with the opposite framing: "Irregular periods are not usually a sign of a problem."
Resolved toward the more cautious reading — argues_against normal_variation — for two reasons. First, the protocol resolves conflict toward higher urgency, and treating irregularity as normal is the lower-urgency reading. Second, the NHS page itself contradicts its own opening line further down, listing "your periods are irregular" under "See a GP if:". Both sources therefore agree on the ACTION even though their prose disagrees, which is exactly why cross-language and cross-source comparison is done on action codes rather than on text.

source_quote: Regular menstrual periods in the years between puberty and menopause are usually a sign that your body is working normally.
note: The clearest positive statement of normality in any source: regularity is framed as a SIGN OF NORMAL FUNCTION, not merely as the absence of a problem. This is the row that makes SELF_CARE reachable.

source_quote: Cramping pain in the lower abdomen (belly) or pelvis
note: Listed by the source among the symptoms of normal menstruation, so mild pain is not in itself a reason to suspect anything. Weak, because the source does not quantify "cramping" and our mild level is a judgement by the user. Important for elimination all the same: without it, any pain at all would push away from SELF_CARE.

source_quote: Irregular or heavy, painful periods are not normal.
A period usually lasts three to seven days and can be light or heavy.
note: Note the second clause: the source explicitly says a normal period "can be light or heavy", so heaviness alone does not argue against normality. Only the extreme does — see the soaking_hourly row below.

source_quote: Prolonged menstrual bleeding occurs when periods regularly last longer than 8 days.
note: MAPPING CAVEAT. The source's threshold is 8 days; our bucket boundary is 7. A period of exactly 8 days falls in our over_7_days bucket but is not yet "prolonged" by this source, so the row fires slightly early. Erring toward abnormality is the safe direction, and the NHS irregular periods page corroborates with a 7-day line: "your periods last longer than 7 days" appears under "See a GP if:".

source_quote: If a cyst does cause symptoms, you may have pressure, bloating, swelling, or pain in the lower abdomen on the side of the cyst.
note: A mass effect, as with fibroids — which is why this feature now supports both and separates them less than it did. The distinguishing detail the source gives, "on the side of the cyst", has no feature; laterality is not something this system asks about.

source_quote: bloating and a swollen tummy
note: Weak: bloating is common and non-specific, and the same NHS page lists it only among symptoms that appear when a cyst is large or has ruptured.

source_quote: If a cyst causes twisting of an ovary, you may have pain along with nausea and vomiting.
note: Weak as evidence, but clinically the important sentence on the page: pain with nausea and vomiting is the torsion picture. It is already covered as an escalation by pelvic_pain_with_nausea_or_vomiting, which is where the urgency comes from; this row only raises the condition.

source_quote: Dull ache in the lower back and thighs
note: The source lists this under "Less common symptoms", so weak. First row to use this feature, which was added in the last batch and had no evidence.

source_quote: If a cyst ruptures, it can cause sudden, severe pain.
note: THE ROW THIS CONDITION WAS ADDED FOR. Sudden onset previously had nothing in the differential to explain it: neither PCOS, endometriosis nor fibroids comes on suddenly. Strong because the source states the mechanism — rupture — rather than listing a symptom.

source_quote: pelvic pain – this can range from a dull, heavy sensation to a sudden, severe and sharp pain
note: Corroborated by the Office on Women's Health: "If a cyst ruptures, it can cause sudden, severe pain." Note the source describes a RANGE, so severity alone raises this condition without mild pain arguing against it.

source_quote: Severe acne which may be hard to treat.
note: Listed, but not framed as characteristic, so weak rather than strong. Acne is common enough in the general population that treating it as strong support would raise PCOS on very little.

source_quote: Skipped periods—called oligomenorrhea
note: Skipped periods lengthen the interval between them. Weak because the source names the pattern rather than a day threshold, so the mapping to our over_35_days bucket is ours.

source_quote: Irregular menstrual cycle. Women with PCOS may miss periods or have fewer periods (fewer than eight in a year). Or, their periods may come every 21 days or more often.
note: PCOS already has a row for over_35_days. This is not a contradiction — the source names BOTH patterns, because the defining problem is absent ovulation rather than a particular cycle length. Worth knowing when reading the grid: for PCOS, cycle length is informative at both extremes and uninformative in the middle.

source_quote: Menstrual irregularities: No menstrual periods—called amenorrhea
note: Absent periods are named explicitly, not merely implied by "irregular".

source_quote: Irregular or missed menstrual periods.
note: Listed first among the symptoms of PCOS, and corroborated by NICHD, which calls absence of ovulation a characteristic feature.

source_quote: Because the characteristic features of PCOS (also known as Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovary Syndrome [PMOS])—absence of ovulation, indicated by irregular menstrual periods or no periods at all; high androgen levels; and growths in one or both ovaries, often clumps of ovarian follicles that have stopped developing—are wide ranging, so, too, are the symptoms of the condition.
note: THE ELIMINATION ROW. The source frames absence of ovulation as a CHARACTERISTIC feature and states it is indicated by irregular or absent periods, so regular cycles argue against — this is explicit framing, not inference from a symptom list, which the protocol forbids. MedlinePlus corroborates diagnostically: "People with PCOS usually have at least two of these problems: Not ovulating...". Without this row PCOS never drops out of the differential and elimination does not work.

source_quote: Infertility. PCOS is one of the most common causes of infertility. But many women with PCOS can still get pregnant.
note: Weak despite strong language, because the same sentence qualifies it: "many women with PCOS can still get pregnant". The source states a population-level association, not a per-person sign.

source_quote: Too much hair on the face, chest, stomach, or thighs.
note: Named as a main sign on both sources; NICHD calls it hirsutism and ties it to high androgen levels, one of the three characteristic features.

source_quote: Signs that you have high levels of androgens: Extra hair growth on your face, chin, and body (hirsutism) Acne Thinning of scalp hair
note: Strong because the source lists it UNDER the androgen-excess heading, and high androgen levels are one of the three characteristic features of PCOS. That is characteristic framing, not a bare symptom list. Retires a feature that had no source until the Office on Women's Health was added.

source_quote: Obesity, weight gain, or trouble losing weight.
note: IMPERFECT MAPPING, deliberately weak. The source names obesity, which is a state rather than a change, alongside weight gain, which is a change. Our feature captures change only. Weak support reflects that the row covers part of what the source says, not all of it.

source_quote: vaginal discharge that looks, smells or feels unusual for you
note: Corroborated by the Office on Women's Health ("Vaginal discharge that may smell foul") and by CDC, which lists "a smelly discharge" among the symptoms that warrant prompt care. Three sources, and again a feature no phase 1 condition claims.

source_quote: bleeding between periods or after sex
note: Corroborated by CDC. Weak because this feature now appears under endometriosis, fibroids and PID; it narrows the differential barely at all.

source_quote: heavy or painful periods that are unusual for you
note: The qualifier matters: "unusual for you" makes this a change from the user's own baseline rather than an absolute level. Our feature captures the level only, so the row loses the comparison the source draws. Weak accordingly.

source_quote: Irregular menstrual periods
note: Listed without emphasis. Weak, and note it pulls the same direction as PCOS and perimenopause — irregularity is the least discriminating finding in the entire knowledge base.

source_quote: Fever (100.4° F or higher)
note: Named directly among the signs, with a threshold. Strong because none of PCOS, endometriosis or fibroids causes fever, so this feature does almost all its work here — it is the clearest infective signal in the set. The source states the temperature; we do not store it, because our feature is a yes/no and inventing a numeric threshold we cannot ask about would be false precision.

source_quote: PID can come on fast, with extreme pain and fever, especially if it is caused by gonorrhea.
note: Same sentence as the row above, supporting a second cell. NHS gives the other half of the picture — "Your symptoms may start quickly over a few days, or develop slowly and get worse over time" — which is why this is weak: both onsets occur, so sudden onset raises PID a little without gradual onset arguing against it.

source_quote: Promptly see a doctor if you have any genital symptoms such as an unusual sore, a smelly discharge, burning when peeing, or bleeding between periods
note: Weak: "burning when peeing" appears in a list of triggers for seeking care rather than as a characteristic sign, and it is at least as suggestive of a urinary tract infection, which is now its own condition.

source_quote: pain felt deep inside when you have sex
note:
Note the wording — "deep inside" — which matches how the Office on Women's Health distinguishes deep from entrance pain for endometriosis.
WORTH WATCHING: this feature now has rows for endometriosis, fibroids and PID. A feature that supports three of nine conditions separates very little, and its earlier billing as highly discriminating is now clearly wrong. It still earns its place — it raises all three above the rest — but next_question should not expect much from it.

source_quote: PID can come on fast, with extreme pain and fever, especially if it is caused by gonorrhea.
note: Weak because the source qualifies it — "especially if it is caused by gonorrhea" — so extreme pain describes one presentation rather than the condition.

source_quote: Blood in the urine. This is more common in younger women. If you see blood in your urine, tell a doctor or nurse right away.
note: First evidence row for this feature, which until now existed only to key a red-flag clause. Weak because the source names it as a symptom without emphasis; NHS lists it under urgent advice rather than among the ordinary symptoms, which is a stronger claim about urgency than about diagnosis.

source_quote: Having a fever, which may mean the infection has reached your kidneys
note: Weak, and deliberately below the PID fever row, which is strong. The source frames fever as a sign the infection has SPREAD rather than as a sign of a UTI itself. Fever now supports both conditions and remains one of the few features that separates infection from the phase 1 three.

source_quote: pain or a burning sensation when peeing (dysuria)
note:
Listed first among UTI symptoms and corroborated by the Office on Women's Health ("Pain or burning when urinating"). Strong.
Note this feature covers bowels AND urination in one question, so a yes answer does not distinguish which. That imprecision now matters more than it did, because endometriosis claims the same feature for cyclical bowel and bladder pain. Splitting the feature is worth considering.

source_quote: needing to pee more often than usual
note: This is the row that stops urinary frequency pointing at fibroids by default. Both conditions claim it, but a UTI is far commoner, and a differential that omits the common explanation systematically over-suspects the rare one.

source_quote: Feeling “full” in the lower abdomen (belly)—this is sometimes called pelvic pressure
note: A bulk effect, and the most discriminating fibroid feature: neither PCOS nor endometriosis is characterised by a sensation of fullness or pressure. Corroborated by the Office on Women's Health, which lists both "Feeling of fullness in the pelvic area" and "Enlargement of the lower abdomen".

source_quote: Age. Fibroids become more common as women age, especially during the 30s and 40s through menopause. After menopause, fibroids usually shrink.
note: A risk factor, not a presenting sign, so weak. Age is cheap to ask (burden 1) and shifts several conditions at once, which is why it earns its place despite being weak individually.

source_quote: Age. Fibroids become more common as women age, especially during the 30s and 40s through menopause. After menopause, fibroids usually shrink.
Fibroids mainly affect women who have not been through the menopause.
note:
THE ELIMINATION ROW for fibroids, and the NHS states it far more directly than any other source — it is a statement about who the condition affects, not an inference from a symptom being absent, which the protocol forbids. The same page lists "have not reached the menopause" among the causes, and the Office on Women's Health corroborates: "After menopause, fibroids usually shrink."
This is the ONLY elimination lever fibroids have. Because "Fibroids do not always cause symptoms", the absence of any given symptom argues against fibroids far less than it would for a condition that is always symptomatic. MAPPING CAVEAT: 55_plus is a proxy for post-menopausal, and some women reach menopause earlier — the row will miss them.

source_quote: Anemia (when you don’t have enough red blood cells)
note: Named directly as a symptom of fibroids, and the Office on Women's Health ties it explicitly to the bleeding: "Heavy bleeding (which can be heavy enough to cause anemia)". This is what turns heavy bleeding from a description into a question about whether it is having an effect.

source_quote: Heavy or painful periods or bleeding between periods
note: Same sentence as the row above, which is legitimate — one source sentence supports two cells. Weak rather than strong because bleeding between periods appears last in a list of alternatives rather than being emphasised.

source_quote: Heavy or painful periods or bleeding between periods
note: First symptom listed, and corroborated by NICHD ("Heavy bleeding or painful periods") and by the NHS heavy periods page, which names fibroids among the causes.

source_quote: Reproductive problems, such as infertility, multiple miscarriages, and early onset of labor during pregnancy
note: Weak, and deliberately so: the Office on Women's Health calls fibroid infertility "very rare". Infertility also appears under PCOS and endometriosis, so it separates the differential very little.

source_quote: pain or discomfort during sex
note:
ADDED TO CORRECT AN ERROR. Batch 02 asserted that pain during sex distinguished endometriosis because "neither PCOS nor fibroids is characterised by it". The NHS fibroids page lists it plainly among fibroid symptoms, so that was wrong and the grid has to say so.
Weak rather than strong: the NHS lists it without emphasis and the page says "Fibroids do not always cause symptoms", whereas the Office on Women's Health frames it as characteristic for endometriosis. The feature still separates the two, but by degree rather than absolutely.

source_quote: Frequent urination (caused by a fibroid pressing on the bladder)
note: The source states the mechanism, not just the association — a fibroid pressing on the bladder — which is characteristic framing rather than a bare list entry. Note this is FREQUENCY, not difficulty passing urine; difficulty is a red flag and is handled separately.
